newsitem.title: MADAGASCAR: Ratsiraka set for victory in Madagascar poll.
newsitem.headline: Ratsiraka set for victory in Madagascar poll.

text.p: Former military rule Didier Ratsiraka took a virtually unbeatable lead on Monday in Madagascar's presidential election over former president Albert Zafy.
Results from the interior ministry showed Ratsiraka 42,921 votes ahead of Zafy with only an estimated 50,000 votes left to be counted at 605 polling stations out of the 14,542 on the island.

Ratsiraka, a 60-year-old retired admiral and former Marxist who ruled Madagascar for 16 years before losing to Zafy in the last presidential election in 1993, had 1,584,363 votes or 50.69 percent of the vote against 1,541,442 or 49.31 percent for Zafy.
Zafy scheduled a news conference for later in the day where political sources expected him to concede defeat according to the count but denounce it as being rigged in favour of his opponent.
Zafy's supporters accused some interior ministry officials last week of manipulating the results in favour of Ratsiraka. The High Consitutitonal Court has to approve the results and publish them.
Election observers from the Organisation of African Unity, the International Committee of Jurists and the Francophone Agency for Technical and Cultural Cooperation have said the election was normal.
The two-round presidential election was ordered after the National Assembly impeached Zafy, president since 1993, for contravening the constitution and exceeding his powers.
The turnout for the December 29 runoff between the two leading candidates from the 15 who contested the first round was some 49 percent, interior ministry figures showed.
Zafy won the 1993 election after a wave of political unrest and subsequent repression had paralysed the country for months.
Ratsiraka returned from 19 months in voluntary exile in France to contest the election after Zafy's impeachment.
Ratsiraka campaigned on promises of establishing a "humanistic and ecological republic" in Madagascar, the world's fourth largest island where 14 million people live in chronic poverty.
Political squabbling under Zafy since 1993 in the former French colony has frustrated plans to improve life for the islanders, who remain among the poorest people in the world.
